title: Comparing with -er and -est
objectives: I can add -er to compare two things and -est to compare three or more.
I can spell wider, widest, thinner, and thinnest correctly.
I can use size and shape words like wide, deep, steep, thick, and sharp.
I can compare real objects with exact words.
rationale: Each of the eight adjectives takes -er and -est, so children practice the comparing endings with real objects: ponds, hills, books, and pencils. The words come in opposite pairs (wide, deep and shallow, thick and thin, sharp and dull) plus steep, which lets children check meaning by contrasting. The unit also teaches the two spelling patterns children meet most: dropping nothing when a word ends in e (wide, wider) and doubling the last letter in a short word (thin, thinner). It builds on similar, than, and unlike from the compare unit.

passage.title: The Pond and the Hill
paras: Tim and Ana walked to a wide pond. The shallow end was good for splashing, but the middle was deep. A steep hill rose beside the water. A thick tree at the top gave shade.
Ana drew the scene with a sharp pencil and made thin lines. Tim's pencil was dull, so his lines were thicker.

qs.q: What does "shallow" mean in the story?
qs.why: The shallow end was good for splashing, so it is not deep.
The story says his pencil was dull, so his lines were thicker.
The story says a steep hill rose beside the water.

teacher.overview: Children learn eight adjectives that take -er and -est and use them to compare real objects. Spelling is part of the lesson: wide becomes wider, and thin becomes thinner. Revisit similar, than, and unlike while comparing.

notes.va.wide.adj: Wide means big from side to side. Show with hands apart. Wider and widest follow the pattern of adding -r and -st when a word ends in e; write them as wide, wider, widest. Use width as a family word for older learners.
notes.va.deep.adj: Deep means far down. Use a bucket with a ruler. Contrast with shallow. Deep also appears in deep sleep; teach only the far down meaning here.
notes.va.shallow.adj: Shallow is the opposite of deep for water and holes. Use a water table. The sound pattern sh may be hard for some Spanish speakers; practice SHAL-oh slowly.
notes.va.steep.adj: Steep describes a slant. Use a ramp made of a book and a board and roll a toy car. A steeper ramp makes the car go faster.
notes.va.thick.adj: Thick means a large distance between two faces, such as a book or a slice. Use real objects. Thick and thin are opposite for flat things.
notes.va.thin.adj: Thin is the opposite of thick. Teach the doubling pattern: thin, thinner, thinnest, with a double n. Compare string, wire, and paper.
notes.va.sharp.adj: Sharp is safe to talk about with pictures; do not pass around real sharp tools. Sharp also means smart and quick in other settings; keep to the edge and point sense.
notes.va.dull.adj: Dull here means not sharp. In other settings it means boring; the other sense can come up and does not need to be taught. Compare a pencil before and after sharpening.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'Both pencils are long, but this one is thicker. When I compare two things I add -er: thicker. If I compare three, I add -est: thickest. The red marker is the thickest of all three.'
discuss: Which object in the room is the thickest? How do you know?
How can you use the words to tell a friend how to find something?
misconceptions: Children may say more wide or most wide. Model wider and widest and use a chart with three pencils.
Some children forget to double the last letter in thin and write thiner.
Children may say sharp and dull only about knives; show a pencil and a crayon.
extend: Make a class chart with a picture and a sentence for each pair of opposites.
Measure and order five objects from thin to thick.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit similar, than, and unlike while comparing two objects: a pencil is thinner than a marker, and unlike a crayon it has a sharp point.

wida.oral: Hold up two objects. Tell your partner which is thicker or thinner, then add a third object and say which is the thickest or thinnest.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (ancho, profundo, poco profundo, empinado, grueso, delgado, afilado, desafilado) not reviewed by a native speaker; delgado/grueso depend on the object.
Sharp and dull also have other senses (a sharp turn, a dull day); only the cutting sense is taught.
